title: HTTP State Management Mechanism
subtitle: How a website remembers you between requests, written down as browsers and servers actually do it.
summary: HTTP forgets every request as soon as it is answered. This document defines the Set-Cookie and Cookie header fields, which let a server hand a browser a small name/value pair and get it back on later requests. It describes a tidy profile for servers, a far more forgiving set of rules for browsers, and the security and privacy problems cookies carry. It replaces RFC 2965 and deprecates the Cookie2 and Set-Cookie2 headers.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP forgets every request once it is answered. This RFC defines the Set-Cookie and Cookie header fields, which let a server give a browser a small name/value pair and get it back on later requests. It describes a strict profile for servers, a more forgiving set of rules for browsers, and the security and privacy problems of cookies. It replaces RFC 2965.

tldr.problem: HTTP treats every request on its own, so a server cannot tell that two requests came from the same visitor.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends a Set-Cookie header with a name, a value and optional scope attributes. The browser stores it and sends matching cookies back in a Cookie header on later requests.
tldr.outcome: It is the specification behind nearly every login, shopping cart and preference on the web, and it openly documents cookies' weaknesses so servers can use them carefully.

today: Cookies are everywhere: the login on almost every website, the contents of a shopping cart and the language you picked are usually carried by a cookie. Every browser and every HTTP library with a cookie jar, such as the one in curl, implements the parsing and matching rules in this document, and servers use its well-behaved profile when they generate cookies. Browsers have also grown beyond it. They restrict third-party cookies in various ways, and they support extra attributes such as SameSite that this RFC does not define.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP is stateless: a server answers a request and keeps nothing about it. That is awkward for anything that needs memory, such as staying logged in. Cookies fix this. With Set-Cookie a server passes name/value pairs, plus metadata, to a user agent (normally a web browser), and the user agent decides whether to return them in a Cookie header on later requests.

This RFC does not invent anything. As it says, the document "does not create new syntax or semantics beyond those in use today." Before it there were three descriptions of cookies, the Netscape specification, RFC 2109 and RFC 2965, and none of them matched how cookies are really used. RFC 6265 writes down the real behavior, moves RFC 2109 and RFC 2965 to Historic, and deprecates the Cookie2 and Set-Cookie2 headers that RFC 2965 introduced.

It is written for two audiences. Servers SHOULD follow the well-behaved profile in Section 4. User agents MUST implement the more liberal processing rules in Section 5, so that they keep working with existing, sloppy servers.

Two rule sets on purpose: servers are asked to be strict in what they send, while browsers must be lenient in what they accept.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP is stateless, which makes it hard to stay logged in or keep a shopping cart. Cookies add memory. A server sends name/value pairs with Set-Cookie, and the browser may return them in a Cookie header. The RFC documents how cookies actually work today and invents no new syntax.

sections.title: How cookies flow
sections.content:
The exchange has two steps. To store state, the origin server includes a Set-Cookie header in an HTTP response. In later requests, the user agent returns a Cookie request header carrying the cookies it received earlier. The server is free to ignore that header or use it for any purpose of its own.

A server may send Set-Cookie with any response. User agents may ignore it on 100-level responses but must process it on others, including 400 and 500 responses. A server can send several Set-Cookie headers in one response, and it should not fold them into a single header, because the comma character that Set-Cookie uses conflicts with the usual folding rule. The presence of either header does not stop HTTP caches from storing and reusing a response.

The simplest example in the RFC is a session identifier: the server sends Set-Cookie: SID=31d4d96e407aad42 and the user agent later sends Cookie: SID=31d4d96e407aad42. To remove a cookie, the server sends it again with an expiry date in the past, and this works only if the Path and Domain match the original.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends a Set-Cookie header in an HTTP response. On later requests, the browser returns a Cookie header carrying the cookies it stored. The server can use or ignore the header as it likes. A response can carry several Set-Cookie headers, which should not be combined into one.

sections.title: The Set-Cookie header
sections.content:
Section 4.1 defines what a well-behaved server sends. A Set-Cookie header is a cookie-pair (a cookie-name, an equals sign and a cookie-value) followed by zero or more attributes, each separated by a semicolon and a space. The name is an HTTP token. The value is made of printable US-ASCII characters but may not contain whitespace, double quotes (unless wrapping the whole value), commas, semicolons or backslashes. Servers that want to store arbitrary data are told to encode it, for example with Base64.

The attributes are Expires, Max-Age, Domain, Path, Secure and HttpOnly, plus extension attributes, which user agents ignore if they do not recognize them (the cookie itself is kept). Servers should not repeat an attribute, and should not send two Set-Cookie headers with the same cookie name in one response.

Dates in Expires should use the four-digit-year RFC 1123 format, such as Wed, 09 Jun 2021 10:18:14 GMT, because browsers disagree about two-digit years.

The Cookie header sent back is just name=value pairs joined by "; ". Attributes are never returned, so a server cannot tell from the header when a cookie expires, where it applies, or whether it was marked Secure or HttpOnly.
sections.plainLanguage: A Set-Cookie header holds a name, an equals sign and a value, followed by optional attributes separated by semicolons. The attributes are Expires, Max-Age, Domain, Path, Secure and HttpOnly. Values may not contain whitespace, commas, semicolons or backslashes, so arbitrary data should be encoded, for example in Base64.

sections.title: Scope and lifetime
sections.content:
Attributes decide how long a cookie lives and where it is sent. Without any, a cookie is returned only to the exact host that set it and lasts until the user agent's "session" ends.

Expires and Max-Age
Expires gives a date; Max-Age gives a number of seconds. If both appear, Max-Age wins. Either makes the cookie persistent. The user agent may still evict it early.
Domain
Widens the cookie to the named domain and its subdomains, so Domain=example.com covers example.com, www.example.com and www.corp.example.com. A host cannot set a cookie for a sibling such as bar.example.com.
Path
Limits the cookie to a path prefix. If omitted, the default is the directory of the request path. Path is not a security boundary.
Secure
Send the cookie only over a "secure" channel, typically HTTPS. It protects confidentiality only, not integrity.
HttpOnly
Hide the cookie from non-HTTP APIs such as scripts that read document.cookie. It is independent of Secure.

A user agent also rejects a cookie whose Domain would not include the host that sent it, and many reject Domain values that are public suffixes such as com or co.uk.
sections.plainLanguage: Attributes decide how long a cookie lives and where it is sent. Without any, a cookie goes only to the exact host that set it and lasts until the browser session ends. Expires or Max-Age make it persistent, Domain extends it to subdomains, and Path limits it to a path prefix.

sections.title: What a user agent must do
sections.content:
Section 5 is the longest part of the RFC and is written as algorithms, so that independent browsers behave alike. It begins with helpers: a forgiving cookie-date parser that tokenizes the date and picks out time, day, month and year in any order, domain matching, and path matching.

Domain matching says a host matches a domain if they are identical, or if the domain is a suffix of the host, the character just before that suffix is a dot, and the host is a name rather than an IP address. A request path matches a cookie path if they are identical, or if the cookie path is a prefix that ends in a slash or is followed by a slash in the request path.

When a cookie arrives the user agent parses the name and value (splitting at the first =; a cookie with no name is ignored), then each attribute. It stores name, value, expiry time, domain, path, creation time, last-access time and flags for persistent, host-only, secure-only and http-only. A new cookie with the same name, domain and path replaces the old one but keeps the old creation time.

When building a Cookie header, the user agent selects cookies whose domain, path, Secure and HttpOnly conditions fit the request, SHOULD list longer paths first and, among equal paths, earlier creation times first, and sends a single Cookie header.
sections.plainLanguage: Browsers follow detailed algorithms so that they behave alike. They parse dates leniently, match the cookie's domain and path against each request, and store, replace or delete cookies accordingly. They then add matching cookies to the Cookie header of outgoing requests.

sections.title: Limits and privacy
sections.content:
Browsers cannot store unlimited cookies. General-use user agents SHOULD support at least 4096 bytes per cookie (name, value and attributes together), at least 50 cookies per domain, and at least 3000 cookies in total. When a user agent removes excess cookies, it must evict expired cookies first, then cookies from domains with too many, then any, oldest last-access first. Servers should therefore use few, small cookies, since the Cookie header travels with every matching request, and should cope when a cookie goes missing.

Section 7 is blunt about privacy. Cookies let web analytics companies recognize returning visitors. The worry is greatest for third-party cookies, set when a page pulls in content from another server, such as an ad network. That server can recognize the same user on every site embedding it. User agents may block sending or accepting such cookies, and the RFC "does not endorse any particular third-party cookie policy." It also notes that two collaborating servers can often track users without cookies by putting identifiers in URLs.

User agents SHOULD let people view, delete and disable cookies. When cookies are disabled they must neither send nor process them. Servers SHOULD choose sensible expiry times; the RFC suggests two weeks as reasonable for a session identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Browsers limit stored cookies: at least 4096 bytes per cookie, 50 per domain and 3000 in total. When over the limit, they evict expired cookies first. Servers should use few, small cookies, because the Cookie header travels with every matching request. Third-party cookies raise the greatest privacy concern.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists cookies' weaknesses openly. Cookies are ambient authority: the browser attaches them to any request, even one a hostile page triggered, which is the root of cross-site request forgery. Cookies sent over plain HTTP travel in the clear, so servers using HTTPS should set Secure on every cookie; otherwise an active attacker can redirect a request to http:// and the browser will include the cookies anyway.

Weak confidentiality
Cookies are not isolated by port or by scheme, and not always by path, because scripts can see them.
Weak integrity
A sibling subdomain can overwrite a cookie scoped to the parent domain, and a network attacker can inject cookies into an HTTPS site by forging an HTTP response.
Session identifiers
Store a random identifier, not the data. Guard against session fixation, where an attacker plants a known identifier in the victim's browser.
Reliance on DNS
If DNS is compromised, cookie protections can fail.

Signing and encrypting cookie contents helps but cannot stop an attacker replaying a genuine cookie. Servers should also not trust that cookies will stay: an attacker can force evictions by flooding the cookie store.
sections.plainLanguage: Cookies have known weaknesses. Browsers attach them to any request, even one triggered by a hostile page, which enables cross-site request forgery. Cookies sent over plain HTTP travel unencrypted, so HTTPS sites should set Secure. A sibling subdomain can overwrite a cookie set for the parent domain.

sections.title: Registrations and succession
sections.content:
The RFC updates the permanent message header registry: Cookie and Set-Cookie are registered with status "standard" for the http protocol, pointing to Sections 5.4 and 5.2. Cookie2 and Set-Cookie2 are listed with status "obsoleted," still pointing at RFC 2965.

The Cookie2 line of work, RFC 2109 (1997) and then RFC 2965 (2000), tried to add versioned, more structured cookies, but did not describe what servers and browsers really did. Practice stayed with the older Cookie and Set-Cookie headers, and RFC 6265 is the reconciliation. The RFC also leaves some matters to implementers: it does not define what a "secure" channel is beyond saying HTTPS typically qualifies, and it leaves the notion of a session to the user agent.

The RFC Editor's index lists RFC 6265 as a Proposed Standard from the httpstate working group.
sections.plainLanguage: Cookie and Set-Cookie are registered with status "standard", while Cookie2 and Set-Cookie2 are marked obsolete. RFC 2109 and RFC 2965 tried to add versioned cookies but did not match real practice. This RFC records what servers and browsers actually do.

items.text: Persistent-flag, host-only-flag, secure-only-flag and http-only-flag record how it may be used.

items.text: The cookie-value is opaque to this RFC; servers give it meaning.
